title: Compliance — SOC 2, HIPAA, GDPR, PCI-DSS, EU AI Act, ISO 42001

questions.question: Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 postponed the EU AI Act's high-risk deadlines. When do obligations for Annex III high-risk systems begin?
options: August 2, 2026, the date originally set before the postponement
December 2, 2027, the postponed deadline for Annex III systems
August 2, 2028, the postponed deadline for Annex I systems
February 2, 2025, the date prohibited AI practices took effect
questions.explanation: The lesson notes that Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 postponed the original August 2026/2027 dates: high-risk obligations now apply from December 2, 2027 for Annex III systems and August 2, 2028 for Annex I systems.

questions.question: Which two-tier fine ceiling does the EU AI Act define?
options: Up to €1M flat for any violation, a single fixed ceiling rather than the Act's turnover-linked structure
Up to €100K for any violation, an amount far below what Article 99 actually sets as the ceiling
No financial penalties, only takedown orders — the Act relies on removal orders rather than fines
Up to €15M or 3% global annual turnover for high-risk-system obligations (Art. 99(4)); up to €35M or 7% for prohibited AI practices (Art. 99(3))
questions.explanation: The lesson states Article 99 sets up to €15M or 3% of global annual turnover for breaches of high-risk-system obligations (Art. 99(4)) and up to €35M or 7% for prohibited AI practices (Art. 99(3)), whichever is higher.

questions.question: Why is post-processing PII cleanup not a defensible GDPR posture?
options: The model already saw the data, so real-time inference-layer redaction (before the LLM call) is the defensible 2026 standard
It is too slow at scale, a performance concern rather than the defensibility issue the lesson raises
GDPR forbids redaction entirely, treating any PII masking approach as non-compliant regardless of timing
Post-processing is identical to real-time in the lesson's framing, so timing does not affect defensibility
questions.explanation: The lesson argues that redacting PII after the LLM has already seen it does not undo the exposure, so real-time inference-layer redaction -- entity recognition and tokenization before the LLM call -- is the defensible 2026 standard, and post-processing claims have failed at audit.

questions.question: What is the practical difference between SOC 2 Type I and Type II?
options: Type I requires HIPAA BAA, a requirement the lesson does not attach to either SOC 2 tier
Type I is more rigorous than Type II, exactly backwards from how the lesson distinguishes the two SOC 2 report tiers
Type I attests controls designed and documented; Type II attests controls operating effectively over 6-12 months
Type II is for startups only, a customer-size distinction the lesson does not draw between the tiers
questions.explanation: The lesson defines Type I as attesting that controls are designed and documented, while Type II attests that those controls operated effectively over a 6-12 month window -- and states B2B procurement in 2026 defaults to requiring Type II.

questions.question: What does cross-framework control mapping aim to deliver?
options: Eliminating audits entirely, since the lesson treats cross-framework mapping as a way to skip procurement review
One control policy that satisfies multiple framework requirements (e.g. access logging maps to ISO 27001 A.5.15-5.18, GDPR Art. 32, HIPAA §164.312(a))
Replacing all frameworks with ISO 42001, consolidating SOC 2, HIPAA, and GDPR into one single standard
More distinct controls per framework, adding overhead rather than reducing audit fatigue
questions.explanation: The lesson's mapping table shows one control, like access logging, satisfying ISO 27001 A.5.15-5.18, GDPR Art. 32, and HIPAA §164.312(a) simultaneously, which reduces audit fatigue instead of maintaining a separate control per framework.

questions.question: What does the lesson recommend for HIPAA + LLM workloads?
options: Never send PHI to an external AI service without a signed BAA; all three hyperscalers and major LLM API providers offer BAAs
HIPAA does not apply to LLMs, since the lesson treats model inference as outside HIPAA's covered-entity scope
Use only on-prem models, never managed, since the lesson treats every managed platform as HIPAA-incompatible
Ship PHI to any provider; BAA is optional as long as the provider encrypts data in transit
questions.explanation: The lesson states PHI cannot be sent to an external AI service without a signed Business Associate Agreement, and notes that Bedrock, Azure OpenAI, Vertex, and the direct OpenAI and Anthropic APIs all offer BAAs -- so the requirement is confirming one, not avoiding managed services.
